CODERED ’26

NTT DATA Track A
Verified AI Modernization of Legacy Code
AI for Software Engineering and Application Modernization on Google Cloud

PURPOSE  Build a working product that helps a modernization engineer understand, translate or test a legacy code module, and prove with executable evidence that the result preserves the original behaviour.
How to use this brief

Choose one focused modernization task within this track. Teams are free to select the legacy language, target stack, supporting tools and interface. A small module with a reproducible equivalence test is sufficient; the suggested directions below are starting points.
1. Challenge Overview
Company / Partner Name:  NTT DATA – Google Cloud Business Unit. Please use NTT DATA for public track naming and branding.
Challenge Title:  NTT DATA Track A: Verified AI Modernization of Legacy Code
Industry / Track:  AI for Software Engineering and Application Modernization, including legacy code comprehension, code translation, test generation and cloud-native re-platforming on Google Cloud.
Challenge Contact:  [Name], [Designation], NTT DATA Google Cloud Business Unit | [email@nttdata.com]
Challenge Type:  Product Innovation / New Product Development. Teams may extend an existing open-source tool when they clearly identify their own new contribution.

Brief Summary:  Build a working product that uses Google Gemini models to help an engineer understand, translate or test a legacy code module, and show with executable tests that the modernized output behaves the same as the original. Choose one module, one modernization step and one measurable outcome, and compare against a stated baseline. Suggested directions include COBOL-to-Java or Python translation, business-rule extraction, characterization test generation and stored-procedure refactoring.

Final offline sprint: 3–4 December 2026, as stated by the organiser. Rounds 1 and 2 use each team’s own Gemini API free-tier access; any finalist credits are to be confirmed before teams rely on them.
2. Industry Context

Large enterprises in banking, insurance, government, telecom and manufacturing still run core processes on decades-old code written in COBOL, PL/I, RPG, older Java EE frameworks or database stored procedures. Much of this code has little documentation, few automated tests and a shrinking pool of engineers who understand it. Moving these systems to cloud-native platforms such as containers on Cloud Run or GKE is a significant part of NTT DATA’s work with Google Cloud clients, and the slowest, riskiest steps are understanding what the old code does and proving that the new code does the same thing.

Large language models can read and write code across many languages, but a plausible translation is not the same as a correct one. This track asks teams to pair a Gemini model with tools that check its work, such as compilers, test runners, coverage tools and side-by-side execution. The aim is a useful prototype that a modernization engineer could try on a small real module.
3. Problem Statement

How can AI help a modernization engineer move a legacy module one step closer to a cloud-native target, while giving reviewers executable evidence that business behaviour has been preserved? Each team should choose one user, one modernization bottleneck and one measurable outcome.

Problem and users:  Modernization engineers and analysts spend substantial time reading undocumented code, reconstructing business rules and writing tests before any code can safely be changed. Choose a concrete bottleneck rather than treating “legacy modernization” as the problem.

When and where:  At a defined step of a realistic modernization project, such as assessing a module before migration, translating one batch program, documenting the rules inside a stored procedure or building a safety-net test suite before refactoring.

Current limitations:  Manual analysis is slow and depends on scarce experts. Rule-based conversion tools can produce code that is hard to maintain, while one-shot AI translations can compile yet silently change behaviour in edge cases such as rounding, date handling, fixed-width records or error paths. Identify the specific limitation in the selected baseline.

Evidence required:  Substantiate the chosen problem with a representative public code sample, cited industry material or practitioner feedback. Demonstrate value using the same legacy inputs, test data and evaluation conditions for the prototype and the baseline.
Suggested problem directions

Legacy batch translation with output parity. Help an engineer translate a small COBOL or similar batch program to Java, Python or Go, then run the original and translated versions on the same input files and compare outputs. A suitable outcome is a higher share of records with identical output, or less time to reach full parity.

Business-rule extraction. Help an analyst turn a legacy module into a readable specification of business rules, with each rule linked to the source lines it came from. Evaluate precision and recall against a hand-labelled set of rules for the same module.

Characterization test generation. Help a developer generate tests that capture the current behaviour of an untested legacy module before it is changed. Measure line or branch coverage achieved and the share of generated tests that pass on the unmodified code.

Stored-procedure refactoring. Help a developer move logic from database stored procedures into an application service, checking that query results match on a sample database. Measure result parity and the number of procedures converted without manual fixes.

Service decomposition support. Help an architect propose service boundaries for a small monolith, grounded in its call graph and data-access patterns. Evaluate against a documented reference decomposition or expert review.
Teams may also propose other modernization problems with a clear user, a legacy artefact and an executable evaluation method.
4. Target Users and Stakeholders

Primary users:  Modernization engineers, application developers, business analysts and solution architects working on legacy-to-cloud programmes. Each team must select a specific user and workflow step.

Secondary users / stakeholders:  Application owners, QA and test leads, security reviewers, platform engineering teams, and enterprises in banking, insurance, public sector and manufacturing that run legacy systems.

Current user journey or workflow:  The team inventories the legacy application, reads code to understand behaviour, documents business rules, writes or recovers tests, translates or refactors code, compares results and deploys to the target platform. Teams should identify the step they will improve.

Key user pain points:  Scarce legacy-language skills, missing documentation, few or no automated tests, AI-generated code that is hard to review, and the risk of silent behaviour changes reaching production.
5. Product Opportunity
The product should help its chosen user move from a legacy artefact to a checked output that can be used in the next step of a modernization project.
User outcome:  Complete a defined modernization step on a real legacy module, inspect the test or comparison evidence, and see clearly which parts still need human review.
Meaningful improvement:  Show a relevant improvement in correctness, speed, test coverage or reviewer effort relative to the stated baseline. Teams choose the metric that fits their task.

Distinct value:  Combine the model with a verification loop, such as compile, run, compare and repair, and with traceability back to the source. Explain the contribution beyond a single prompt to a chat interface or an existing conversion tool.
6. Expected Product Capabilities

Must-have capabilities:  A working user workflow on at least one real legacy module; meaningful use of at least one Google Gemini model inside the product, through the Gemini API or Vertex AI; an executable check of the output, such as tests, output comparison or compilation; traceability from generated output back to source lines; and a repeatable evaluation script. Using Gemini only as a coding assistant while building the project does not demonstrate Gemini-powered product functionality.

Nice-to-have capabilities:  Repair loops that feed test failures back to the model; agent orchestration, for example with Google’s open-source Agent Development Kit; deployment of the modernized service to Cloud Run or a local container; confidence or risk flags per function; reviewer-friendly diff views; and history across repeated attempts.

Expected user interactions:  A user supplies a legacy module and its test inputs, reviews the proposed output alongside the evidence, and can accept, edit or reject each change. Teams choose their own interface and architecture.

Expected demonstration / deliverable:  A GitHub repository accessible for review; a README showing where Gemini is used and which model powers each feature; and a short working demo. Include setup instructions, the legacy sample and its licence, a reproducible test case, baseline results, limitations and known failure cases.
7. Technical and Operational Constraints

Technical or platform constraints:  Free-tier Gemini API limits vary by model and project and are shown in the Google AI Studio rate-limit console rather than as fixed published figures; check them before development and again before the final sprint. Some models, such as certain Pro, image and video models, may not be available on the free tier. Handle HTTP 429 and temporary service errors with bounded retries, backoff and a clear failure state. Legacy toolchains, such as the open-source GnuCOBOL compiler, must run in the team’s own environment.

Performance, accuracy, or latency requirements:  Teams define task-specific targets and compare against a stated baseline on a documented test set. Report correctness, such as output parity or test pass rate, alongside time, token usage and cost per module. Report every run, including failures, not only the best one.

Security, privacy, or compliance requirements:  Keep API keys server-side or in protected local configuration, never in repositories or demos. Use only public open-source, self-written or synthetic code and data with a compatible licence; do not use client, employer or NTT DATA proprietary code. Free-tier Gemini API requests may be used by Google to improve its products, so send nothing confidential. Flag generated code that touches security-sensitive logic for human review.

Hardware, connectivity, or deployment limitations:  API calls require internet access. Teams provide their own computing environment, compilers and runtimes. No mainframe, licensed conversion product or private NTT DATA system is provided. Small modules of a few hundred to a few thousand lines and local execution are acceptable.

Budget or resource constraints:  Rounds 1 and 2 use the Gemini API free tier under its current availability and limits, through each team’s own Google account. [To be confirmed: any Google Cloud or Gemini API credits for finalist teams, the amount per team or member, and activation dates.] Teams should not build their project around unconfirmed credits and should plan experiments within free-tier limits.

Domain-specific safety requirements:  Generated code is a proposal, not a validated result. A human must review and approve changes before they would be merged or deployed. The prototype must not be presented as production-ready or as certified equivalent to the original system.
8. Available Resources and Support
The following support applies to this track. Unconfirmed items are marked at the relevant field; teams should not build their project around them.

APIs, SDKs, developer tools, or technology credits:  Rounds 1 and 2: Gemini API free tier through Google AI Studio, with each team creating its own key. Teams may also use Vertex AI in their own Google Cloud projects at their own cost. Google’s Agent Development Kit and Gen AI SDKs are open source and optional. [To be confirmed: finalist credits and how they will be allocated.]

Sample datasets or permitted data sources:  Teams may use public open-source legacy code under compatible licences, programs they write themselves and public sample datasets. NTT DATA is not providing client code or proprietary datasets. Teams must document the source and licence of every sample.

Sandbox environments or test infrastructure:  Teams may build local test environments using containers and open-source compilers. A dedicated event sandbox, Google Cloud project or reserved model capacity is not currently committed. [To be confirmed.]
Documentation and reference materials:  Public Gemini API, Vertex AI, Agent Development Kit and Cloud Run documentation, and open-source legacy toolchains such as GnuCOBOL [1–5].

Mentors, domain experts, or technical sessions:  NTT DATA Google Cloud modernization practitioners may offer an online briefing and remote mentoring, subject to availability and separate confirmation. [To be confirmed: whether NTT DATA staff will attend the final offline sprint in person.]

Other resources or support:  No additional rewards are currently committed. [Optional: add any recognition, interview opportunity or certification support NTT DATA wishes to offer, with its selection method and deadline.]
9. Business and Adoption Context
Teams should explain who could use the product after the event and what evidence would justify a small follow-up test.
Intended customer or beneficiary:  Modernization delivery teams at systems integrators and the enterprises they serve, such as banks, insurers and public-sector bodies that run legacy applications.

Current alternatives or competing solutions:  Manual analysis and rewrite, commercial code-conversion tools, or a single-prompt AI translation with no verification. Teams must name an appropriate alternative and compare the same module under similar conditions.

Potential value created:  Shorter analysis and conversion time per module, fewer behavioural defects found late in testing, better-documented business rules and less dependence on scarce legacy skills. Teams should quantify the benefit their prototype actually demonstrates.

Potential adoption pathway:  Validate the prototype with a modernization practitioner, document remaining gaps and identify a small follow-up test on a larger or more complex public code base. Further discussion with NTT DATA teams is possible by mutual interest and is not guaranteed.

Commercial or operational considerations:  Estimate token cost and time per module or per thousand lines processed, required tooling and integration effort. Consider code ownership, data residency and human review at larger scale. Any credits support prototyping and do not establish future production pricing.

Known assumptions or uncertainties:  Public legacy samples are smaller and cleaner than real enterprise systems. Expert feedback may be limited. Credit availability, mentor participation and any follow-up collaboration remain to be confirmed. Model availability and free-tier limits may change.
10. Success Indicators

Success should be demonstrated on a bounded task with a stated baseline, reproducible inputs and relevant measurements. These indicators guide the brief; the organiser must confirm the final judging rules.
Functional outcomes:  Demonstrate an end-to-end workflow on a reproducible legacy module, including actual Gemini model use, execution-based checking and handling of invalid inputs or API failure.

User or customer outcomes:  Explain who benefits and compare effort, review time or confidence with the current workflow. Include practitioner feedback where available; identify assumptions where it is unavailable.

Technical performance indicators:  Report a relevant baseline and metric, such as output parity across test records, test pass rate, branch coverage, rule-extraction precision and recall, or the number of manual fixes needed. Include limitations and failures, not only the best run.
Business or operational indicators:  Report approximate cost and time per completed module and explain what a small pilot on a larger code base would require.

Safety, reliability, or compliance indicators:  Show code and data provenance, protected credentials, clear marking of unverified output and appropriate human review. Distinguish generated suggestions from tested results. Report retries and failures for workflows that depend on external APIs.
11. Scope and Boundaries

In scope:  A focused modernization step on a real or realistic legacy module with meaningful Gemini model use, a working prototype and executable evaluation. Teams may use open-source tools, compilers and Google Cloud services as permitted by their licences and event rules.

Out of scope:  A generic chat wrapper around code; a concept deck without working functionality; claims of full-application migration or guaranteed equivalence; or use of proprietary or client code. Mainframe hardware, licensed conversion products and production deployment are not required.

Permitted assumptions or simplifications:  Small modules, synthetic input files, simplified file or database I/O, local containers instead of cloud deployment and a subset of language features. State assumptions, label prerecorded demonstrations and disclose how the simplified test differs from a real migration.

Dependencies:  Gemini API access under each team’s own account; internet access; permitted code samples and toolchains; organiser submission rules; and confirmation of credits, mentoring and judging participation.
12. Industry Engagement

Will the company provide mentors or subject-matter experts?  NTT DATA Google Cloud modernization practitioners may offer an online briefing and remote mentoring, subject to availability and separate confirmation. [To be confirmed: whether NTT DATA staff will attend the final offline sprint in person.]
Will teams receive feedback during development?  Online feedback may be considered. The channel, timing and reviewers require separate confirmation with the organiser.
Will the company participate in evaluation or demonstrations?  [To be confirmed: whether NTT DATA representatives will join judging or demonstrations in person or remotely.]

Is further validation, pilot discussion, or product exploration possible after the event?  Yes, as a possible follow-up for promising projects. Practitioner reviews, validation or further exploration depend on mutual interest and separate agreement; no placement, funding or commercial engagement is promised.
Any follow-on engagement is subject to mutual interest and separate agreement.
13. Intellectual Property and Participation Terms
Project review, publicity and any later collaboration should use explicit terms communicated to participants before development begins.

Data and resource usage conditions:  Use Google services under the applicable Google terms, and third-party code or data only with the necessary rights. The organiser should not collect API keys or passwords.

Confidentiality requirements, if any:  Build submissions with information that may be shared with reviewers. NTT DATA will not provide confidential material for this track. Any restricted repository access must be agreed in advance. Additional event confidentiality terms are to be confirmed.

Intellectual property and ownership terms:  Project ownership remains with the participants. Participation does not automatically transfer project ownership or commercial rights to NTT DATA or Google. Final participation terms should state any review permissions needed. Teams must respect the licences of any open-source code or data they use.

Restrictions on using company names, data, or materials:  Use the NTT DATA and Google Cloud names accurately to describe the challenge and the integration. Do not imply that NTT DATA or Google has endorsed, certified or deployed a project. Obtain participants’ permission before NTT DATA features project descriptions, screenshots or demos, and credit the teams.

Terms governing subsequent collaboration:  Pilots, licensing, investment, employment, commercial use or further collaboration require a separate agreement. Final reward and participation terms must be communicated before participants rely on them.
14. Partner Contact and Clarifications
Primary contact:  [Name], [Designation], NTT DATA Google Cloud Business Unit
Email:  [email@nttdata.com]
Reference documentation / resource links:  Public references are listed below. Teams should recheck model availability, limits and pricing before development.
[1] Gemini API documentation, rate limits and pricing: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs
[2] Vertex AI generative AI documentation: https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs
[3] Agent Development Kit (open source): https://google.github.io/adk-docs/
[4] Cloud Run documentation: https://cloud.google.com/run/docs
[5] GnuCOBOL open-source compiler: https://gnucobol.sourceforge.io/

Clarification process:  Send track, credit and reward questions to the NTT DATA contact, coordinating event-wide questions through the organiser. Gemini API platform issues should go through Google’s public developer support channels, with redacted error details. Clarifications affecting eligibility or judging should be shared consistently with all teams.
Submission Checklist
☒  The problem is real, relevant, and clearly stated.
☒  Target users and desired outcomes are identified.
☒  Teams have freedom to develop their own solutions.
☒  A working prototype is reasonably achievable within the challenge timeline.
☒  Business value and adoption can be evaluated.
☒  Technical constraints and available resources are stated.
☐  Data, safety, confidentiality, and IP terms are clear.
☐  Evaluation expectations are communicated consistently.
THE GUIDING PRINCIPLE
The company defines the opportunity. The team defines the solution.

CODERED ’26

NTT DATA Track B
AI Incident Investigation for Cloud-Native Systems
AI for Cloud Operations and Site Reliability Engineering on Google Cloud

PURPOSE  Build a working product that helps an on-call engineer find the likely cause of a failure in a cloud-native application faster, with every conclusion backed by evidence from logs, metrics, traces or configuration.
How to use this brief

Choose one focused operations problem within this track. Teams are free to select the application, telemetry stack, supporting tools and interface. A narrow incident type with a reproducible fault-injection test is sufficient; the suggested directions below are starting points.
1. Challenge Overview
Company / Partner Name:  NTT DATA – Google Cloud Business Unit. Please use NTT DATA for public track naming and branding.
Challenge Title:  NTT DATA Track B: AI Incident Investigation for Cloud-Native Systems

Industry / Track:  AI for Cloud Operations and Site Reliability Engineering, including incident investigation, root-cause analysis, alert triage and guarded runbook automation on Google Cloud and Kubernetes.
Challenge Contact:  [Name], [Designation], NTT DATA Google Cloud Business Unit | [email@nttdata.com]
Challenge Type:  Product Innovation / New Product Development. Teams may extend an existing open-source tool when they clearly identify their own new contribution.

Brief Summary:  Build a working product that uses Google Gemini models to help an on-call engineer investigate incidents in a microservices application, citing specific evidence for each conclusion and keeping a human in charge of any fix. Choose one incident type, inject reproducible faults into an open-source application, and measure diagnosis accuracy and time against a stated baseline. Suggested directions include root-cause localization, alert grouping, change-aware investigation, evidence-backed postmortems and guarded runbook execution.

Final offline sprint: 3–4 December 2026, as stated by the organiser. Rounds 1 and 2 use each team’s own Gemini API free-tier access; any finalist credits are to be confirmed before teams rely on them.
2. Industry Context

Enterprises are moving critical services onto Kubernetes and serverless platforms such as GKE and Cloud Run. These systems produce large volumes of logs, metrics, traces and events across many services, and a single fault can trigger alerts in several places at once. NTT DATA builds and operates such platforms for Google Cloud clients, where the time taken to identify the cause of an incident directly affects customer impact and service-level commitments.

Language models can read varied telemetry and summarise it, but an investigation is useful only if its conclusions can be checked and its actions are safe. This track asks teams to connect a Gemini model to real observability data and tools, test it against faults whose cause is known in advance, and keep a human in control of any change.
3. Problem Statement

How can AI help an on-call engineer reach a correct diagnosis faster, while showing the evidence behind each conclusion and never taking a risky action on its own? Each team should choose one user, one investigation bottleneck and one measurable outcome.

Problem and users:  On-call engineers and SREs spend substantial time switching between dashboards, log queries and runbooks to work out which service and which change caused an incident. Choose a concrete bottleneck rather than treating “operations” as the problem.

When and where:  At a defined stage of incident response on a realistic microservices system, such as the first minutes after an alert, grouping related alerts, identifying the faulty service or writing the postmortem.

Current limitations:  Dashboards show symptoms rather than causes, alert storms hide the original fault, runbooks go out of date, and AI summaries without cited evidence are hard to trust during an incident. Identify the specific limitation in the selected baseline.

Evidence required:  Substantiate the chosen problem with cited SRE material, a representative incident scenario or practitioner feedback. Demonstrate value using the same injected faults, telemetry and evaluation conditions for the prototype and the baseline.
Suggested problem directions

Root-cause localization. Given an alert and the surrounding telemetry, identify the faulty service and the likely cause, such as a crashed pod, injected latency, a bad configuration or resource exhaustion, citing specific log lines, metric windows or trace spans. A suitable outcome is higher top-1 or top-3 accuracy, or less time to a correct diagnosis.

Alert grouping and noise reduction. Group alerts that share a cause into one incident with a plain-language explanation. Measure grouping accuracy against the known injected faults and the reduction in items an engineer must review.
Change-aware investigation. Link an incident to a recent deployment or configuration change using commit history and Kubernetes events. Evaluate on scenarios where a known bad change was introduced.

Guarded runbook execution. Turn a written runbook into proposed diagnostic or remediation steps that run only after human approval, preferably as a dry run first. Measure steps completed correctly and unsafe actions blocked.

Evidence-backed postmortem drafting. Produce a timeline and draft postmortem from incident data, with every statement linked to its source. Evaluate factual accuracy against the known fault and the reviewer edits required.
Teams may also propose other operations problems, such as cloud cost-anomaly investigation or SLO breach forecasting, with a clear user and evaluation method.
4. Target Users and Stakeholders
Primary users:  On-call engineers, site reliability engineers, platform engineers and DevOps teams running cloud-native applications. Each team must select a specific user and workflow step.
Secondary users / stakeholders:  Incident commanders, application owners, service-desk teams, security operations, and enterprises that operate services under availability commitments.

Current user journey or workflow:  An alert fires; the engineer acknowledges it, checks dashboards, queries logs and traces, looks for recent changes, forms and tests hypotheses, applies a fix, confirms recovery and writes a postmortem. Teams should identify the step they will improve.
Key user pain points:  Alert storms, fragmented telemetry tools, knowledge held by a few experts, outdated runbooks, pressure to act quickly and low trust in automated conclusions.
5. Product Opportunity
The product should help its chosen user move from an alert or incident to a checked diagnosis or action that can be used in the next step of incident response.
User outcome:  Reach a diagnosis or decision on a defined incident type, inspect the evidence behind it, and see clearly what remains uncertain and what requires human approval.

Meaningful improvement:  Show a relevant improvement in diagnosis accuracy, time to diagnosis, alerts reviewed or postmortem quality relative to the stated baseline. Teams choose the metric that fits their task.

Distinct value:  Combine the model with tool access to real telemetry, an evidence trail for each conclusion and safe human-in-the-loop controls. Explain the contribution beyond pasting logs into a chat interface or relying on existing monitoring alerts.
6. Expected Product Capabilities

Must-have capabilities:  A working user workflow on a running microservices application with reproducible injected faults; meaningful use of at least one Google Gemini model inside the product, through the Gemini API or Vertex AI; conclusions linked to specific telemetry evidence; human approval before any change to the system; and a repeatable evaluation script over a documented set of fault scenarios. Using Gemini only as a coding assistant while building the project does not demonstrate Gemini-powered product functionality.

Nice-to-have capabilities:  Agent orchestration with tool calls to log, metric, trace and Kubernetes APIs, for example using Google’s open-source Agent Development Kit; integration with Google Cloud Observability or open-source tools such as Prometheus, Grafana or Jaeger; dry-run remediation; uncertainty scores; investigation history; and evaluation across several fault types.

Expected user interactions:  A user supplies an alert or incident, follows the investigation, reviews the cited evidence, can confirm, correct or reject the diagnosis, and approves or blocks any proposed action. Teams choose their own interface and architecture.

Expected demonstration / deliverable:  A GitHub repository accessible for review; a README showing where Gemini is used and which model powers each feature; and a short working demo. Include setup instructions, the target application and fault-injection scripts, the scenario set with known causes, baseline results, limitations and known failure cases.
7. Technical and Operational Constraints

Technical or platform constraints:  Free-tier Gemini API limits vary by model and project and are shown in the Google AI Studio rate-limit console rather than as fixed published figures; check them before development and again before the final sprint. Some models, such as certain Pro, image and video models, may not be available on the free tier. Handle HTTP 429 and temporary service errors with bounded retries, backoff and a clear failure state. Telemetry can be large, so teams should filter, summarise or retrieve relevant data rather than sending everything to the model, and should report the context sizes they use.

Performance, accuracy, or latency requirements:  Teams define task-specific targets and compare against a stated baseline on a documented scenario set, for example at least 10 injected faults across at least 3 fault types. Report accuracy alongside time to diagnosis, token usage and cost per incident. Report every scenario, including misses.

Security, privacy, or compliance requirements:  Keep API keys and cluster credentials server-side or in protected local configuration, never in repositories or demos. Give the product least-privilege, read-only access by default. Use only telemetry generated in the team’s own test environment or public datasets with compatible licences; do not use production logs from any employer or client. Free-tier Gemini API requests may be used by Google to improve its products, so send nothing confidential and redact secrets that appear in logs.

Hardware, connectivity, or deployment limitations:  API calls require internet access. Teams provide their own computing environment; a laptop running a local Kubernetes cluster such as kind or minikube, or Docker Compose, is acceptable. No production cluster, paid monitoring product or private NTT DATA system is provided.

Budget or resource constraints:  Rounds 1 and 2 use the Gemini API free tier under its current availability and limits, through each team’s own Google account. [To be confirmed: any Google Cloud or Gemini API credits for finalist teams, the amount per team or member, and activation dates.] Teams should not build their project around unconfirmed credits and should plan experiments within free-tier limits.

Domain-specific safety requirements:  The product must not change any system without explicit human approval. Remediation demonstrations must run only against the team’s own test environment. Diagnoses are hypotheses until confirmed, and the prototype must not be presented as autonomous operations or production-ready.
8. Available Resources and Support
The following support applies to this track. Unconfirmed items are marked at the relevant field; teams should not build their project around them.

APIs, SDKs, developer tools, or technology credits:  Rounds 1 and 2: Gemini API free tier through Google AI Studio, with each team creating its own key. Teams may also use Vertex AI in their own Google Cloud projects at their own cost. Google’s Agent Development Kit and Gen AI SDKs are open source and optional. [To be confirmed: finalist credits and how they will be allocated.]

Sample datasets or permitted data sources:  Teams may use telemetry generated from open-source demo applications they run themselves, such as Google’s Online Boutique microservices demo or the OpenTelemetry Demo, together with open-source fault-injection tools such as Chaos Mesh or their own scripts, and public incident datasets with compatible licences. NTT DATA is not providing client telemetry or proprietary datasets. Teams must document data provenance.

Sandbox environments or test infrastructure:  Teams may build local clusters or use their own Google Cloud projects at their own cost. A dedicated event sandbox, GKE cluster or reserved model capacity is not currently committed. [To be confirmed.]

Documentation and reference materials:  Public Gemini API, Vertex AI and Agent Development Kit documentation; Google’s Site Reliability Engineering books, available free online; and documentation for the chosen demo application and fault-injection tool [1–7].

Mentors, domain experts, or technical sessions:  NTT DATA Google Cloud SRE and platform engineering practitioners may offer an online briefing and remote mentoring, subject to availability and separate confirmation. [To be confirmed: whether NTT DATA staff will attend the final offline sprint in person.]

Other resources or support:  No additional rewards are currently committed. [Optional: add any recognition, interview opportunity or certification support NTT DATA wishes to offer, with its selection method and deadline.]
9. Business and Adoption Context
Teams should explain who could use the product after the event and what evidence would justify a small follow-up test.

Intended customer or beneficiary:  Platform, SRE and managed-services teams at systems integrators and enterprises running cloud-native applications, particularly where service-level commitments apply.

Current alternatives or competing solutions:  Manual investigation using dashboards and log search, rule-based alert correlation in existing monitoring tools, or a single prompt to an AI model with raw logs. Teams must name an appropriate alternative and compare the same scenarios under similar conditions.

Potential value created:  Shorter time to diagnosis, fewer alerts for engineers to review, more consistent investigations across experience levels and better-documented postmortems. Teams should quantify the benefit their prototype actually demonstrates.

Potential adoption pathway:  Validate the prototype with an SRE or platform practitioner, document remaining gaps and identify a small follow-up test on a larger application or richer fault set. Further discussion with NTT DATA teams is possible by mutual interest and is not guaranteed.

Commercial or operational considerations:  Estimate token cost and time per investigated incident, telemetry access and integration effort, and how cost scales with log volume. Consider data residency, access control and human review at larger scale. Any credits support prototyping and do not establish future production pricing.

Known assumptions or uncertainties:  Injected faults are cleaner than real incidents, which often have several interacting causes. Expert feedback may be limited. Credit availability, mentor participation and any follow-up collaboration remain to be confirmed. Model availability and free-tier limits may change.
10. Success Indicators

Success should be demonstrated on a bounded task with a stated baseline, reproducible inputs and relevant measurements. These indicators guide the brief; the organiser must confirm the final judging rules.

Functional outcomes:  Demonstrate an end-to-end investigation on a reproducible fault scenario, including actual Gemini model use, cited evidence, the human approval step and handling of missing data or API failure.

User or customer outcomes:  Explain who benefits and compare time, effort or confidence with the current workflow. Include practitioner feedback where available; identify assumptions where it is unavailable.

Technical performance indicators:  Report a relevant baseline and metric, such as top-1 and top-3 root-cause accuracy, time to correct diagnosis, alert-grouping accuracy, share of claims supported by cited evidence, or unsafe actions blocked. Include limitations and missed scenarios, not only the best run.
Business or operational indicators:  Report approximate cost and time per investigated incident and explain what a small pilot on a larger environment would require.

Safety, reliability, or compliance indicators:  Show least-privilege access, protected credentials, redaction of sensitive log content, clear uncertainty and mandatory human approval for changes. Distinguish hypotheses from confirmed causes. Report retries and failures for workflows that depend on external APIs.
11. Scope and Boundaries

In scope:  A focused incident-response step on a running microservices application with known injected faults, meaningful Gemini model use, a working prototype and measurable evaluation. Teams may use open-source tools and Google Cloud services as permitted by their licences and event rules.

Out of scope:  A generic chat wrapper around logs; a concept deck without working functionality; autonomous changes to any system without approval; use of real production telemetry; or claims of production readiness. Large clusters and paid observability products are not required.

Permitted assumptions or simplifications:  Small applications, local clusters, synthetic traffic, a limited set of fault types and simplified telemetry pipelines. State assumptions, label prerecorded demonstrations and disclose how the simplified test differs from real operations.

Dependencies:  Gemini API access under each team’s own account; internet access; the chosen demo application and tools; organiser submission rules; and confirmation of credits, mentoring and judging participation.
